full_judgment:
2. The opposite parties filed Title Suit No. 225 of 1983 for a permanent injunction restraining the defendants-petitioners, from entering into the suit properties by force. Their case in brief is that plaintiff No.1 Jabangir Alam Matubbar and his brother defendant No. 2 Babar Ali Matubbar and his mother Shamsunnahar Begum defendant No.3 and one Abul Hossain Howlader started a partnership business under the name and style M/s. National Rice Flour and Oil Mills at Hatkhola Road, Barisal. Subsequently Abul Hossain Howlader retired on 23.4.77. The National Rice Flour and Oil Mills Ltd., a private limited company was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913 on 23 4.77 and it took over the aforesaid partnership business on that day on 27.2.83 defendant No. Ithe father of plaintiff No. 1 a Director of the Company, and three other defendants offered I to sell their entire shares to plaintiff No. 1 and his wife plaintiff No. 2.The offer was accepted and instruments of transfer of shares were executed by the parties. The transfers were approved in a meeting of the Board of Directors held on 11.3.83. The documents of transfers were duly filed with the Registrar, Joint Stock Companies. After transferring the entire shares, defendants 1-4 ceased to be members of the company with effect from 11.3.83. On 29.4.83 at about 11.00 a. m. the defendants along with some hired goondas fell upon the suit properties, but due to timely intervention and the intercession of the local people they could not succeed in their objectives. Apprehending a serious breach of peace the plaintiffs filed the suit for permanent injunction. They also filed an application for temporary injunction. 

 3. The petitioners in their written objection contended that the plaintiffs had no prima facie case and the suit was barred under Section 3 of the Companies Act; that the alleged transfers of shares were false and papers to that effect were created by forgery; that a proceeding under section 137 of the Companies Act as to the genuineness of the instruments of transfer and other papers were pending before the Registrar, Joint Stock Companies. It was further asserted that the plaintiffs did not file the necessary papers in support of their case. On 29.6.83 the trial Court returned the plaint after finding that it had no jurisdiction to bear the matter as the matter in dispute was to be adjudicated by the High Court Division of the Supreme Court under the Companies Act, 1913. The plaintiffs filed an appeal against that order. They also filed an application for temporary injunction. On 27.7.83 the learned District Judge passed the following impugned order:- 

 4. The petitioner's main contention is that the learned District Judge violated the mandatory provisions of rule 3 of Order 39 of the Code of Civil Procedure as no notice was directed to be served on them. It has been pointed out that at the trial court the defendants filed some interrogatories, but the plaintiff, did not answer to that. They also sought discovery of some documents from the plaintiffs but no papers were filed on the plea that the relevant papers were lying with Registrar, Joint Stock Companies. It is submitted that apart from the illegality of the impugned order the plaintiffs failed to make out prima facie case for any restraining order like the impugned one. 

 5. On behalf of the opposite parties it is contended that the present petition is misconceived as no revisional application lies from the impugned order. It has been pointed out that the appeal before the learned District Judge was against an order returning the plaint and the impugned order was passed under clause (r) of rule 1 of Or. 413 and hence the petitioners, if they were at all aggrieved, could have filed a First Miscellaneous Appeal. It is submitted that sub-section (2) of section 104 of the Code of Civil Procedure which provides that no appeal shall lie from any order passed in appeal under that section is applicable to tin appeal against a final order adjudicating a dispute between the parties and not relating to an order, as in the present case returning the plaint to the plaintiff without adjourning the matter in dispute between the parties. My attention has also been drawn to paragraph 20 of the written objection filed by the present petitioners at the trial Court against the plaintiffs application for temporary injunction where it is stated that the entire suit properties are under the enjoyment and possession of the plaintiffNos. 1 and 2 and the defendants as Directors and defendants No. 1 as the Managing Director from this it is submitted that as possession of plaintiffs 1 and 2 are admitted they are entitled to hold on there and the defendants are to be directed to maintain status quo in the suit properties. It is further contended that the petitioners instead of rushing to this Court ought to have exhausted their remedy available to them under Order 39 rule 4 as the impugned order did not attain its finality and it could be discharged, varied or set aside by the learned District Judge. 

 8. Apprehending that the impugned order may be set aside on the ground of illegality the plaintiffs have filed an application for temporary Injunction in this Court. From the plea dings of the parties it appears that the disputed properties belong to a limited company, but the company has not been impleaded in this suit. Though the plaintiffs are claiming that the defendants ceased to be members and defendant No. 1 also ceased to be the Managing Director of the Company there is no sufficient material placed on record in this regard. If defendant No.1 had already ceased to be the Managing Director it is not disclosed who has been appointed as the Managing Director in his place. An investigation under section 137 of the Companies Act is pending before the Registrar. After hearing the learned Advocates and perusing the papers I hold that the plaintiffs-opposite parties have not made out a prima facie case for an order of temporary injunction. An order for maintenance of status quo is also not called for in the facts and circumstances of the case. Observations in this judgment are confined to this proceeding only.
